newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Date pencilled in for start of tv conciliation.
newsitem.headline: Date pencilled in for start of tv conciliation.

text.p: The European Parliament and Council of Minister have pencilled in March 20 to start the conciliation procedure on revisions to the Television Without Frontiers directive, 89/552/EEC, EU officials said on Monday.
But before it can go ahead, reservations by Spain and Germany on the Commission's proposal for a Council position on televised sports events will have to be ironed out, they said.

The Commission -- seeking a breakthrough on a key European Parliamentary demand -- proposed in February a system aimed at ensuring viewers are not deprived of at least a handful of major sports events when they are snapped up exclusively by pay television stations.

At last week's meeting of the Committee of Permanent Representatives (COREPER), Spain baulked at a clause in the proposal on retroactivity, which would mean that it would come into force only on the day the directive was adopted.

EU officials said that Spain's demand endangered the Commission's position, which was struck in consultation with industry, which has already snapped up exclusive rights to a number of future sporting events.

Under the Commission's proposal, member states would be able to demand in-the-clear viewing of a national list of important sporting events like the World Cup and Olympic Games, even where exclusive rights to these games had been snapped up.
Germany also expressed its usual reservations about whether the federal government has competence to agree the plan, as normally its laender have the power to deal with such audiovisual matters.
In the case of televised sport, laender are free to decide on their own systems for ensuring availability of major sporting events.

No major move is expected from the Council and Commission within the conciliation procedure on the second major amendment demanded by the European Parliament in its second reading on the revised Television without Frontiers directive in November.
That demand is for a so-called V-Chip to be installed in new television stations to allow parents to screen out violent programmes from their children.

The Commission and the member states say that as it is technically not feasible to meet the parliament's demand, and the parliament, having been met half-way on the issue of sport on television, does not seem to be turning up the pressure, officials said.
Once conciliation talks between the Parliament and the Council start, both sides have six weeks to reach an agreement.
